claim: A considerable proportion of COVID-19 infected people continue to experience symptoms after their initial recovery.

claim: Convalescent COVID-19 patients were discharged after 15 days (median [interquartile range, IQR 11–26]).

evidence: This is a direct report of data from the study cohort.

claim: Half of the selected convalescent COVID-19 patients (n = 30) had at least one cardiovascular risk factor.

source: Overall, CEC attributes of convalescent COVID-19 patients correlated with a vast majority of differentiation and activation factors associated with T cells and B cells (IL-4, IL-5, IL-7, IL-17A, IL-18, MIP-1α, and RANTES) (Turner et al., 2014), implicating a broad adaptive immune response with endothelial dysfunction.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis and citation to Turner et al., 2014.

claim: The correlation of CEC attributes with T and B cell differentiation and activation factors implicates a broad adaptive immune response with endothelial dysfunction.
source: Overall, CEC attributes of convalescent COVID-19 patients correlated with a vast majority of differentiation and activation factors associated with T cells and B cells (IL-4, IL-5, IL-7, IL-17A, IL-18, MIP-1α, and RANTES) (Turner et al., 2014), implicating a broad adaptive immune response with endothelial dysfunction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis showing associations between CEC attributes and immune activation factors.

claim: Endothelial cells, once activated, could also be a source of cytokines, which in turn could activate their immune counterparts.
source: Besides being a target of the immune mediators, we recognize that endothelial cells, once activated, could also be a source of these cytokines, which in turn could activate their immune counterparts.
evidence: This is established knowledge about endothelial cell function.

claim: Counter receptors ITGAL, SELPLG, and CX3CR1 were most pronouncedly expressed by CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and to some extent monocytes.
source: We found that those counter receptors were most pronouncedly expressed by CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and to some extent monocytes (Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published single-cell transcriptomic data presented in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of CX3CR1 was intensified in mild and severe COVID-19 patients than healthy participants.
source: In Wilk et al.'s dataset, the expression of CX3CR1 was intensified in mild and severe COVID-19 patients than healthy participants (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published single-cell transcriptomic data from Wilk et al., presented in Figure 4a.

claim: A higher proportion of NK or both CD8+ and NK cells expressing all three counter receptors was found in mild and severe COVID-19 samples, respectively, regardless of comorbidity with cardiovascular disease.
source: The relationship between counter receptors expression and COVID-19 disease was even more marked in Schulte-Schrepping et al.'s dataset with a higher proportion of NK or both CD8+ and NK cells expressing all three counter receptors found in mild and severe COVID-19 samples, respectively, regardless of comorbidity with cardiovascular disease (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published single-cell transcriptomic data from Schulte-Schrepping et al., presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of counter receptors ITGAL, SELPLG, and CX3CR1 generally marks cytotoxic effector lymphocytes in peripheral blood.
source: As the presence of those counter receptors generally marks cytotoxic effector lymphocytes in peripheral blood (Nishimura et al., 2002), we correspondingly found that CD8+ T cells and NK cells were the major cytotoxic populations expressing perforin and granzymes (Figure 4b), especially in COVID-19 patients (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nishimura et al., 2002.

claim: CD8+ T cells and NK cells were the major cytotoxic populations expressing perforin and granzymes.
source: As the presence of those counter receptors generally marks cytotoxic effector lymphocytes in peripheral blood (Nishimura et al., 2002), we correspondingly found that CD8+ T cells and NK cells were the major cytotoxic populations expressing perforin and granzymes (Figure 4b), especially in COVID-19 patients (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published single-cell transcriptomic data presented in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Convalescent COVID-19 patients, in particular those with underlying cardiovascular risk, had significantly higher frequencies of effector CD8+ and CD4+ T cells (EM) than healthy controls.
source: Therefore, we analyzed T cell features by immunophenotyping in our cohort (Carissimo et al., 2020) and found that convalescent COVID-19 patients, in particular those with underlying cardiovascular risk, had significantly higher frequencies of effector CD8+ and CD4+ T cells (EM), and central memory CD8+ T cells (CD8 CM) than healthy controls (Figure 5a), while there were no notable differences across the groups for absolute numbers of circulating CD8+/CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunophenotyping data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: Convalescent COVID-19 patients, in particular those with underlying cardiovascular risk, had significantly higher frequencies of central memory CD8+ T cells (CD8 CM) than healthy controls.
source: Therefore, we analyzed T cell features by immunophenotyping in our cohort (Carissimo et al., 2020) and found that convalescent COVID-19 patients, in particular those with underlying cardiovascular risk, had significantly higher frequencies of effector CD8+ and CD4+ T cells (EM), and central memory CD8+ T cells (CD8 CM) than healthy controls (Figure 5a), while there were no notable differences across the groups for absolute numbers of circulating CD8+/CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunophenotyping data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: There were no notable differences across the groups for absolute numbers of circulating CD8+/CD4+ T cells.
source: Therefore, we analyzed T cell features by immunophenotyping in our cohort (Carissimo et al., 2020) and found that convalescent COVID-19 patients, in particular those with underlying cardiovascular risk, had significantly higher frequencies of effector CD8+ and CD4+ T cells (EM), and central memory CD8+ T cells (CD8 CM) than healthy controls (Figure 5a), while there were no notable differences across the groups for absolute numbers of circulating CD8+/CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunophenotyping data presented in Figure 5a.

claim: There is a possibility that individuals recovered from COVID-19 could be susceptible to vascular injury due to effector T cell cytotoxicity.
source: There is a possibility that individuals recovered from COVID-19 could be susceptible to vascular injury due to effector T cell cytotoxicity (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed higher frequencies of effector T cells in convalescent patients.

claim: About 2.5% of convalescent COVID-19 patients are found with thrombosis (including arterial and venous events), 30 days post discharge.
source: About 2.5% of convalescent COVID-19 patients are found with thrombosis (including arterial and venous events), 30 days post discharge (Patell et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patell et al., 2020.

claim: COVID-19 convalescents had significantly higher CEC count than non-COVID-19 healthy participants.
source: Our findings reveal that COVID-19 convalescents had significantly higher CEC count than non-COVID-19 healthy participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study.

claim: The compounded effects of COVID-19 and prior cardiovascular risk factors rendered the most pronounced endothelial activation markers in COVID-19 convalescents.
source: In comparison with non-COVID-19 patients with cardiovascular risk (i.e., hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia), the compounded effects of COVID-19 and prior cardiovascular risk factors rendered the most pronounced endothelial activation markers in COVID-19 convalescents.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study comparing different patient groups.

claim: Activated endothelial cells are likely to release cytokines, which trigger extrinsic coagulation pathway.
source: Activated endothelial cells are likely to release cytokines, which trigger extrinsic coagulation pathway (Coccheri, 2020), suggesting that recovered individuals may be susceptible to risk of thrombotic complications.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Coccheri, 2020.

claim: Recovered individuals may be susceptible to risk of thrombotic complications.
source: Activated endothelial cells are likely to release cytokines, which trigger extrinsic coagulation pathway (Coccheri, 2020), suggesting that recovered individuals may be susceptible to risk of thrombotic complications.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of activated endothelial cells and their potential to trigger coagulation.

claim: Cytokine production remained heightened post-infection in COVID-19 patients.
source: The sequence of events leading to post-COVID-19 complication has not been fully elucidated, but likely a vicious cycle caused by vascular leakage, activation of coagulation pathway, and inflammation (Teuwen et al., 2020). In this study, our cytokine profiling confirmed that cytokine production remained heightened post-infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine profiling data from the study.

claim: Significantly higher proportions of effector CD8+ and CD4+ T cells were found in COVID-19 convalescents, especially those with pre-existing cardiovascular risk, than healthy participants.
source: We also found significantly higher proportions of effector CD8+ and CD4+ T cells in our COVID-19 convalescents, especially those with pre-existing cardiovascular risk, than healthy participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunophenotyping data from the study.

claim: Prolonged overactive state of the immune system could be implicated with endothelial dysfunction.
source: Collectively, these suggest that prolonged overactive state of the immune system could be implicated with endothelial dysfunction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations of persistent cytokine production and higher proportions of effector T cells.

claim: In many COVID-19 convalescents, broad CD8+ T-cell response against multiple SARS-CoV-2 proteins mediated by effector and memory T cell populations were detected.
source: In many COVID-19 convalescents, broad CD8+ T-cell response against multiple SARS-CoV-2 proteins mediated by effector and memory T cell populations were detected, suggesting a key role for T cells in protective immunity in recovered patients (Dan et al., 2021; Grifoni et al., 2020; Oxford Immunology Network Covid-19 Response T cell Consortium et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dan et al., 2021; Grifoni et al., 2020; Oxford Immunology Network Covid-19 Response T cell Consortium et al., 2020.

claim: Broad CD8+ T-cell response in COVID-19 convalescents suggests a key role for T cells in protective immunity in recovered patients.
source: In many COVID-19 convalescents, broad CD8+ T-cell response against multiple SARS-CoV-2 proteins mediated by effector and memory T cell populations were detected, suggesting a key role for T cells in protective immunity in recovered patients (Dan et al., 2021; Grifoni et al., 2020; Oxford Immunology Network Covid-19 Response T cell Consortium et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of broad CD8+ T-cell responses, supported by citations.

claim: Majority of SARS-CoV-2 reactive T cells in COVID-19 convalescents had phenotypic markers of TEMRA.
source: It was reported that majority of these SARS-CoV-2 reactive T cells in COVID-19 convalescents had phenotypic markers of TEMRA (Dan et al., 2021) known to be more differentiated and cytotoxic in nature.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dan et al., 2021.

claim: TEMRA cells are known to be more differentiated and cytotoxic in nature.
source: It was reported that majority of these SARS-CoV-2 reactive T cells in COVID-19 convalescents had phenotypic markers of TEMRA (Dan et al., 2021) known to be more differentiated and cytotoxic in nature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TEMRA cells.

claim: CD8+ T cells in COVID-19 patients were associated with cytotoxic genes, as well as receptors that might potentially interact with counter receptors/ligands on activated endothelial cells.
source: Here, our analysis of published scRNA-seq datasets demonstrated that CD8+ T cells in COVID-19 patients were associated with cytotoxic genes, as well as receptors that might potentially interact with counter receptors/ligands on activated endothelial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: Activated endothelial cells in COVID-19 convalescents could become a target of cytotoxic effector T lymphocytes.
source: This led us to hypothesize that activated endothelial cells in COVID-19 convalescents could become a target of cytotoxic effector T lymphocytes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observations of activated endothelial cells and cytotoxic T cells with appropriate receptors.

claim: Endothelial injury could result in vascular permeability, further exposing tissue factor from underneath, which predisposes to risk of blood clotting.
source: Endothelial injury could result in vascular permeability, further exposing tissue factor from underneath, which predisposes to risk of blood clotting (van Hinsbergh, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to van Hinsbergh, 2012.

claim: Immune cell-mediated endothelial injury has been observed in Ebola infection.
source: Immune cell-mediated endothelial injury has been observed in other viral infections, including Ebola, human cytomegalovirus infection, and malaria, where T cells recruited to infected site by inflammation could induce apoptosis of infected endothelial cells, causing vascular leakage (Claser et al., 2019; van de Berg et al., 2012; Wolf et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Claser et al., 2019; van de Berg et al., 2012; Wolf et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2000.

claim: Immune cell-mediated endothelial injury has been observed in human cytomegalovirus infection.
source: Immune cell-mediated endothelial injury has been observed in other viral infections, including Ebola, human cytomegalovirus infection, and malaria, where T cells recruited to infected site by inflammation could induce apoptosis of infected endothelial cells, causing vascular leakage (Claser et al., 2019; van de Berg et al., 2012; Wolf et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Claser et al., 2019; van de Berg et al., 2012; Wolf et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2000.

claim: Immune cell-mediated endothelial injury has been observed in malaria.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Claser et al., 2019; van de Berg et al., 2012; Wolf et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2000.

claim: T cells recruited to infected site by inflammation could induce apoptosis of infected endothelial cells, causing vascular leakage.
source: Immune cell-mediated endothelial injury has been observed in other viral infections, including Ebola, human cytomegalovirus infection, and malaria, where T cells recruited to infected site by inflammation could induce apoptosis of infected endothelial cells, causing vascular leakage (Claser et al., 2019; van de Berg et al., 2012; Wolf et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Claser et al., 2019; van de Berg et al., 2012; Wolf et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2000.

claim: In acute coronary syndrome, cytotoxic CD4+ T cells were capable of causing damages to endothelial cells.
source: Likewise, in non-infectious diseases such as acute coronary syndrome and systemic sclerosis, cytotoxic CD4+ T cells were capable of causing damages to endothelial cells (Maehara et al., 2020; Nakajima et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maehara et al., 2020; Nakajima et al., 2002.

claim: In systemic sclerosis, cytotoxic CD4+ T cells were capable of causing damages to endothelial cells.
source: Likewise, in non-infectious diseases such as acute coronary syndrome and systemic sclerosis, cytotoxic CD4+ T cells were capable of causing damages to endothelial cells (Maehara et al., 2020; Nakajima et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maehara et al., 2020; Nakajima et al., 2002.

claim: Some endothelial cells affected by SARS-CoV-2 infection may have elicited pattern recognition receptors such as toll-like receptors, activating interferon pathway and inflammatory cytokine production that persist to convalescent phase.
source: It is also possible that some endothelial cells affected by SARS-CoV-2 infection had elicited pattern recognition receptors such as toll-like receptors, activating interferon pathway and inflammatory cytokine production that persist to convalescent phase.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism of persistent inflammation.

claim: Antigen-experienced T cells preferentially adhere to activated endothelial cells and undergo transendothelial migration.
source: Antigen-experienced T cells preferentially adhere to activated endothelial cells and undergo transendothelial migration (Carman and Martinelli, 2015; Marelli-Berg et al., 2004), triggering vascular remodeling due to endothelial damage (Cuttica et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carman and Martinelli, 2015; Marelli-Berg et al., 2004.

claim: Antigen-experienced T cells adhering to activated endothelial cells trigger vascular remodeling due to endothelial damage.
source: Antigen-experienced T cells preferentially adhere to activated endothelial cells and undergo transendothelial migration (Carman and Martinelli, 2015; Marelli-Berg et al., 2004), triggering vascular remodeling due to endothelial damage (Cuttica et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cuttica et al., 2011.

claim: Activated and infected endothelial cells could be susceptible to direct cytotoxic T cell-mediated killing due to persistent immune activation in COVID-19 convalescents.
source: Therefore, we postulate that activated and infected endothelial cells could be susceptible to direct cytotoxic T cell-mediated killing due to persistent immune activation in COVID-19 convalescents.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observations of activated endothelial cells and persistent immune activation.

claim: Profiling of CECs may serve as a form of vascular surveillance to complement hematologic assessment in identifying early molecular and endothelial changes in high-risk individuals.
source: Our profiling of CECs may serve as a form of vascular surveillance to complement hematologic assessment in identifying early molecular and endothelial changes in high-risk individuals.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential clinical utility of CEC profiling.

claim: Analysis of CECs may detect subclinical changes in the vasculatures and be able to provide accurate and easily transferable endpoints in clinical assessment.
source: Analysis of CECs may detect subclinical changes in the vasculatures and be able to provide accurate and easily transferable endpoints in clinical assessment.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential clinical utility of CEC analysis.

claim: Endothelial instability may be a key mechanism underpinning the development of post-infection vascular complications.
source: In summary, managing the aftermath of COVID-19 is an imperative. Endothelial instability may be a key mechanism underpinning the development of post-infection vascular complications.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study showing endothelial dysfunction in convalescent patients.

claim: Clinical trials in preventive therapy for vascular complications may be needed.
source: Clinical trials in preventive therapy for vascular complications may be needed.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: CECs were defined by a combined immunophenotypic profile of CD45−/CD31+/CD133−/DNA+.
source: Finally, a nucleic acid stain was used to distinguish anucleate platelets from nucleated CECs, which were defined here by a combined immunophenotypic profile of CD45−/CD31+/CD133−/DNA+ (Burger and Touyz, 2012; Duda et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations to Burger and Touyz, 2012; Duda et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2013.

claim: Putative EPCs were identified by CD133+/CD45−/DNA+ population.
source: As a comparison, putative EPCs were identified by CD133+/CD45−/DNA+ population (Ingram et al., 2004; Mancuso et al., 2020; Rafii and Lyden, 2003).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations to Ingram et al., 2004; Mancuso et al., 2020; Rafii and Lyden, 2003.

claim: ICAM1 is integral for the process of leukocyte adhesion.
source: To further analyze endothelial cell activation, CECs were characterized for the expression of activation markers, namely, intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM1), P-selectin (SELP), and fractalkine (CX3CL1) (Figure 1a), which are integral for the processes of leukocyte adhesion, platelet aggregation, and trans-endothelial migration, respectively (Goncharov et al., 2017; Johnson and Jackson, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goncharov et al., 2017; Johnson and Jackson, 2013.

claim: P-selectin (SELP) is integral for the process of platelet aggregation.
source: To further analyze endothelial cell activation, CECs were characterized for the expression of activation markers, namely, intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM1), P-selectin (SELP), and fractalkine (CX3CL1) (Figure 1a), which are integral for the processes of leukocyte adhesion, platelet aggregation, and trans-endothelial migration, respectively (Goncharov et al., 2017; Johnson and Jackson, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goncharov et al., 2017; Johnson and Jackson, 2013.

claim: Fractalkine (CX3CL1) is integral for the process of trans-endothelial migration.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goncharov et al., 2017; Johnson and Jackson, 2013.

claim: EPC levels are more likely to elevate immediately following thrombotic events when EPCs are mobilized from the bone marrow into the bloodstream to facilitate vascular repair.
source: With regard to EPC counts, no significant difference was observed possibly due to the absence of recent adverse vascular events in our groups with cardiovascular risks. EPC levels are more likely to elevate immediately following thrombotic events when EPCs are mobilized from the bone marrow into the bloodstream to facilitate vascular repair (Massa et al., 2005; Shintani et al., 2001; Valgimigli et al., 2004; Yip et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Massa et al., 2005; Shintani et al., 2001; Valgimigli et al., 2004; Yip et al., 2008.

claim: Measurement of CECs seemed to be able to detect subclinical endothelial dysfunction.
source: Here, measurement of CECs seemed to be able to detect subclinical endothelial dysfunction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CECs were elevated in convalescent patients without recent adverse vascular events.
